## Procedure

**Name the conventional figure and its embedded conventions** (a performance
metric, efficiency, or cost ceiling) before stripping anything.

**Strip each convention back to a governing hard constraint, definition, or
direct measurement.** Name the constraint explicitly (e.g., "the Second Law of
Thermodynamics," "Carnot efficiency bound," "the speed of light in fiber"). A
governing hard constraint is whatever genuinely cannot be negotiated in this
domain — a physical law, a mathematical bound, a conservation identity, a
protocol's minimum round trips. It is often not thermodynamic, and the technique
applies wherever such a constraint exists. Do not reason by analogy to what
others currently achieve — the ceiling is set by the constraint, not by the best
incumbent.

**Derive the limit the fundamentals permit**, using the governing constraint and
first-principles values (constants, definitions, direct measurements). This is
the **ideal bound**: the furthest the figure can go in the improving direction
once every convention is removed and only the constraint remains.

**Use the tightest applicable bound — a valid bound is not automatically the
right one.** The loosest true bound is always available and is nearly always
useless: it is true, unfalsifiable, and overstates headroom, so an analysis
bracketed against it reports far more room than really exists. Ask what else
binds before the ideal ceiling does — materials, cost, a practical operating
point, a regulatory minimum — and bracket against that too.

**Fix the direction before you label anything.** Ask whether improvement means
the figure goes *up* (efficiency, yield, throughput, recovery) or *down*
(energy per unit output, latency, cost, defect rate, time-to-X); the answer
names the bound — an **ideal ceiling** when higher is better, an **ideal
floor** when lower is better — and it fixes the ordering of the bracket and
the sense of both gaps. State the direction in one clause before the bracket,
because an unstated direction is how a floor gets written up as a ceiling.

**Bracket in three tiers.** State each explicitly, and label which is which:

- **Ideal bound** — written as **Ideal ceiling** when higher is better and
  **Ideal floor** when lower is better: what the governing hard constraint
  permits. Derived, not observed. The quantity cannot pass it in the improving
  direction — nothing exceeds the ceiling, nothing falls below the floor.
- **Best demonstrated:** the best figure anyone has actually achieved, **cited**
  — a record, a measured result, a published benchmark. This tier is an
  *observation*, never a calculation.
- **Conventional figure:** what current practice in this context achieves.
  Label the tier **Conventional** — naming the system instead ("this plant",
  "this service") is not the label, and a reader cannot tell a conventional
  tier from an arbitrary aside.

Then state two gaps rather than one, ordered by direction: both gaps run from
current practice toward the bound — increasing when higher is better,
decreasing when lower is better. **Conventional → best demonstrated** is
headroom somebody has already proven reachable, and **best demonstrated →
ideal bound** is headroom nobody has reached yet. The two are different claims
with very different risk, and collapsing them into a single "gap" is what makes
a theoretical-limit analysis sound more actionable than it is.

Identify how much of the gap is irreducible (the constraint imposes it — a
process converting X → Y can never be 100% efficient under the Second Law, and
a signal crossing an ocean can never arrive sooner than light does) versus how
much is convention (headroom the constraint allows but practice has not
reached).

**A model-dependent bound is not a ceiling.** (And, in the minimisation
direction, not a floor.) Many published "limits" are the
answer to a narrower question than the one being asked, and real systems exceed
them. Before using a bound as a tier, ask *what exactly does this bound
constrain, and under what assumptions?* If it is model-dependent, either label
it as an illustrative reference rather than a ceiling, or drop it. The
Curzon-Ahlborn efficiency is the standard cautionary case: it is the efficiency
of an endoreversible engine **at maximum power**, not a maximum efficiency, and
real plants that trade power density for efficiency exceed it — so using it as a
"practical ceiling" understates what is achievable. Put an observed record in the
demonstrated tier instead of a computed one.

**Apply the stop criterion.** The analysis is complete when: (1) the governing
hard constraint is named explicitly, (2) the ideal bound is derived from
first-principles values — not from what competitors achieve, (3) the best
demonstrated figure is cited as an observation, and (4) both gaps are stated
explicitly. A theoretical-limit analysis that names a bound without bracketing
those gaps is incomplete — the bracket, not the ceiling alone, is the
deliverable.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a given bash command and returns its output.

The working directory persists between commands, but shell state does not. The shell environment is initialized from the user's profile (bash or zsh).

IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user:

 - Read files: Use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
 - Edit files: Use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
 - Write files: Use Write (NOT echo >/cat <<EOF)
 - Communication: Output text directly (NOT echo/printf)
While the Bash tool can do similar things, it’s better to use the built-in tools as they provide a better user experience and make it easier to review tool calls and give permission.

# Instructions
 - If your command will create new directories or files, first use this tool to run `ls` to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location.
 - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes in your command (e.g., cd "path with spaces/file.txt")
 - Try to maintain your current working directory throughout the session by using absolute paths and avoiding usage of `cd`. You may use `cd` if the User explicitly requests it. In particular, never prepend `cd <current-directory>` to a `git` command — `git` already operates on the current working tree, and the compound triggers a permission prompt.
 - You may specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). By default, your command will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
 - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. You do not need to use '&' at the end of the command when using this parameter. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 600000ms / 10 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
 - For git commands:
  - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
  - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
  - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.
 - Avoid unnecessary `sleep` commands:
  - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
  - Use the Monitor tool to stream events from a background process (each stdout line is a notification). For one-shot "wait until done," use Bash with run_in_background instead.
  - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — use `run_in_background`. No sleep needed.
  - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause.
  - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
  - Long leading `sleep` commands are blocked. To poll until a condition is met, use Monitor with an until-loop (e.g. `until <check>; do sleep 2; done`) — you get a notification when the loop exits. Do not chain shorter sleeps to work around the block.
 - When running `find`, search from `.` (or a specific path), not `/` — scanning the full filesystem can exhaust system resources on large trees.
 - When using `find -regex` with alternation, put the longest alternative first. Example: use `'.*\.\(tsx\|ts\)'` not `'.*\.\(ts\|tsx\)'` — the second form silently skips `.tsx` files.


# Committing changes with git

Only create commits when requested by the user. If unclear, ask first. When the user asks you to create a new git commit, follow these steps carefully:

You can call multiple tools in a single response. When multiple independent pieces of information are requested and all commands are likely to succeed, run multiple tool calls in parallel for optimal performance. The numbered steps below indicate which commands should be batched in parallel.

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
   - Run git status after the commit completes to verify success.
   Note: git status depends on the commit completing, so run it sequentially after the commit.
4. If the commit fails due to pre-commit hook: fix the issue and create a NEW commit

Important notes:
- NEVER run additional commands to read or explore code, besides git bash commands
- NEVER use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- DO NOT push to the remote repository unless the user explicitly asks you to do so
- IMPORTANT: Never use git commands with the -i flag (like git rebase -i or git add -i) since they require interactive input which is not supported.
- IMPORTANT: Do not use --no-edit with git rebase commands, as the --no-edit flag is not a valid option for git rebase.
- If there are no changes to commit (i.e., no untracked files and no modifications), do not create an empty commit
- In order to ensure good formatting, ALWAYS pass the commit message via a HEREDOC, a la this example:
<example>
git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
   Commit message here.
   EOF
   )"
</example>

# Creating pull requests
Use the gh command via the Bash tool for ALL GitHub-related tasks including working with issues, pull requests, checks, and releases. If given a Github URL use the gh command to get the information needed.

IMPORTANT: When the user asks you to create a pull request, follow these steps carefully:

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel using the Bash tool, in order to understand the current state of the branch since it diverged from the main branch:
   - Run a git status command to see all untracked files (never use -uall flag)
   - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed
   - Check if the current branch tracks a remote branch and is up to date with the remote, so you know if you need to push to the remote
   - Run a git log command and `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to understand the full commit history for the current branch (from the time it diverged from the base branch)
2. Analyze all changes that will be included in the pull request, making sure to look at all relevant commits (NOT just the latest commit, but ALL commits that will be included in the pull request!!!), and draft a pull request title and summary:
   - Keep the PR title short (under 70 characters)
   - Use the description/body for details, not the title
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Create new branch if needed
   - Push to remote with -u flag if needed
   - Create PR using gh pr create with the format below. Use a HEREDOC to pass the body to ensure correct formatting. End the body with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.
<example>
gh pr create --title "the pr title" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary
<1-3 bullet points>

## Test plan
[Bulleted markdown checklist of TODOs for testing the pull request...]
EOF
)"
</example>

Important:
- DO NOT use the TaskCreate or Agent tools
- Return the PR URL when you're done, so the user can see it

# Other common operations
- View comments on a Github PR: gh api repos/foo/bar/pulls/123/comments

content.content:
1. "The network is reliable"
2. "Latency is zero"
3. "Bandwidth is infinite"
4. "The network is secure"
5. "Topology doesn't change"
6. "There is one administrator"
7. "Transport cost is zero"
8. "The network is homogeneous"

The list originated at Sun Microsystems. L. Peter Deutsch, a Sun Fellow, first compiled seven of them in 1994, building on four that Bill Joy and Dave Lyon had already identified. James Gosling, another Sun Fellow and Java's inventor, added the eighth around 1997.

The article argues for a **monolith-first** approach: build new applications as monoliths, even if you expect to need microservices later. Early on, speed and fast feedback matter most, and teams rarely draw service boundaries correctly before they understand the domain. Splitting later, once boundaries are clearer, is safer. The author also notes the evidence is still limited and that some practitioners disagree.

On cost, the article says that "even their advocates say that using them incurs a significant MicroservicePremium," and that microservices are therefore "only useful with more complex systems."

Splitting is justified once the monolith has a good modular design and the service boundaries have settled: "as boundaries stabilize, break down into finer-grained services." The author also warns that not every system can be cleanly decomposed.

The CAP theorem, also called Brewer's theorem, holds that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties: consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. Under the article's definitions, consistency means every read returns the latest write (or an error), availability means every request to a non-failing node gets a response, and partition tolerance means the system keeps operating when the network drops or delays messages.

Eric Brewer originally conjectured the result. He presented it as a conjecture at the 2000 Symposium on Principles of Distributed Computing (PODC), after first introducing the idea in 1998–1999. Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch of MIT published a formal proof in 2002, which turned the conjecture into a theorem.

Melvin Conway introduced the law in his paper **"How do Committees Invent?"** in *Datamation*, April 1968. The article's lead says 1967, but the cited publication is from 1968.

The wording, as quoted on the page, is:

> "organizations which design systems"

> "are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations."

The original also includes a parenthetical, "(in the broad sense used here)," which I've omitted for length. The page cites this wording to the *Datamation* paper but doesn't reproduce the paper itself, so this is the best available version from the source.

96	
97	**untested belief** — a claim held as true that has not been empirically verified in the context of this analysis.
98	Prescribed treatment: verify it, or flag it unverified. An untested belief used in a derivation chain must be marked with the `GT-N?` notation (see Ground Truths) and any conclusion depending on it inherits a confidence caveat.
99	
100	### Stakes-Escalation Rule
101	
102	The higher the stakes of the conclusion resting on an assumption, the more that assumption must be pushed toward physical law or verified ground truth status. Classification drives the method — it does not merely label.
103	
104	### Verdict Vocabulary
105	
106	The Verdict cell is a token prefix followed by an em-dash and the justification — the bare
107	token leads so it stays matchable, and the em-dash prose carries the reasoning. **The separator
108	is an em-dash, never a colon.** `Accept: the figure is audited` puts the token and the reasoning
109	on one side of a punctuation mark that appears throughout ordinary prose, so the cell stops being
110	matchable — which is the whole property the token-first form exists to provide. Measured: a single
111	run using the colon form scored ten non-conforming verdict cells at once. The em-dash is not a
112	stylistic preference here; it is the delimiter:
113	
114	- **Accept** — the assumption survives challenge and may be used in the analysis (e.g., "Accept — survives P2 challenge; physical-law backed by GT-1")
115	- **Challenge** — the assumption is questionable; probe further before use (e.g., "Challenge — vendor benchmark unverified, flagged GT-5?")
116	- **Discard** — the assumption is false or irrelevant; remove from the reasoning chain (e.g., "Discard — contradicted by GT-2, no longer load-bearing")
117	
118	**A current-constraint verdict records its expiry at the point of use.** An assumption classified `current constraint` is accepted only until that constraint lapses; the verdict cell says when. The expiry belongs in the em-dash justification and never in the token slot — the token slot carries one of the three tokens above and nothing else.
119	
120	**Conforming — a current constraint recording its expiry:**
121	
122	```text
123	Accept — expires at term end (1 or 3 years); until then the constraint is contractual, not physical
124	```
125	
126	**Non-conforming — the expiry hoisted into the token slot:**
127	
128	```text
129	Current constraint (expires at term end) — contractual, not physical
130	```
131	
132	The vocabulary above is unchanged because run 3 rendered four current-constraint rows conformingly on the identical prompt by putting the expiry in the justification — this is a worked example, not a schema change.

136	## 3. Ground Truths
137	
138	List the irreducible, verified facts the analysis builds on. Each ground truth carries a stable identifier used by the Derivation Chains section. Once assigned, an ID does not change.
139	
140	A ground truth must pass this test: it is a fact that is true regardless of what solution is chosen, verifiable independently of the analysis, and not derived from another item on this list.
141	
142	Every ground truth carries a **provenance label** answering one question: *did this analysis read the asserted figure or wording in the cited source?* The answer decides the suffix. A citation being present is not verification — a citation can name a real document and be wrong about what is in it.
143	
144	**Verified ground truth form** (provenance `read-at-source` — no suffix):
145	
146	- **GT-1** [fact text] — source: [verification source — data, measurement, published spec, direct observation]; read-at-source: [page, table, section, or quoted passage where the figure was read]
147	- **GT-2** [fact text] — source: [verification source]; read-at-source: [where read]
148	
149	**Delegate-reported ground truth form** (provenance `reported-by-delegate` — `?` required):
150	
151	- **GT-3?** [fact text] — cited to: [source the delegate named]; reported-by-delegate: [which sub-agent, search, or summary supplied it] — cited source not opened by this analysis
152	
153	**Unverified ground truth form (D-07)** (provenance `unverified` — `?` required):
154	
155	- **GT-4?** [fact text] — unverified: [specific reason the fact could not be verified in this analysis]
156	
157	The `?` suffix signals that this ground truth has not been read at its source — whether because it is an untested belief or because a delegate reported it and nobody opened the citation. Any conclusion depending on a `GT-N?` input inherits a confidence caveat in the Derivation Chains section. The analysis may proceed with such inputs — but the uncertainty must be visible.
158	
159	**The `?` is the default.** Drop it only when the read-at-source location can be named. A delegate report counts as read-at-source only when it quotes the source's own wording and that quote was checked — not when it merely supplies a well-formed citation.
160	
161	**Provenance summary (required):** enumerate the `?`-marked ground truths **by ID**, and for every unsuffixed ground truth feeding a load-bearing chain — one a conclusion this analysis presents rests on, whatever its band — name its read-at-source location. This is the same population the Phase 3 exit criterion names: scoping it to HIGH chains would let an unread figure excuse itself, because the `?` it takes caps its chain below HIGH. Write the list, not a number:
162	
163	```text
164	?-marked: GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14 (4 of 22)
165	Read-at-source: GT-3 — 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)(i), subsections (A)/(B)/(R) quoted verbatim
166	```
167	
168	A stated integer does not satisfy this — an integer cannot be checked against the list it summarizes, and an enumeration can. Where a count and its enumeration disagree, **the enumeration governs.** Neither an empty enumeration nor a count of zero satisfies this on its own; the named locations are the auditable part.
169	
170	IDs are stable once assigned. GT-3 remains GT-3 throughout the document even if GT-3 is later verified or discarded.

174	## 4. Derivation Chains
175	
176	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
177	
178	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
179	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
180	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a
181	Conclusion-section (section 6) claim back to the chain in this section that established it.
182	
183	**Chain format:**
184	
185	```text
186	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
187	```
188	
189	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
190	
191	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
192	
193	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.
194	
195	```text
196	GT-1 ([brief fact label]) + GT-6 ([brief fact label])
197	→ [intermediate claim]
198	→ [further intermediate]
199	→ [conclusion]
200	```
201	
202	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
203	
204	```text
205	GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])
206	→ [intermediate claim]
207	→ [conclusion]
208	```
209	
210	The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
211	
212	The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples.
213	
214	**Conforming — head, then one hop per line:**
215	
216	```text
217	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
218	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
219	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
220	```
221	
222	**Non-conforming — a hop broken across physical lines:**
223	
224	```text
225	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
226	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
227	  once idle-time billing is included
228	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
229	```
230	
231	The continuation line does not begin with `→`, so the chain terminates at the head's first hop and what remains reads as an incomplete chain.
232	
233	**Non-conforming — the same hops rendered as a numbered list:**
234	
235	```text
236	1. GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
237	2. Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
238	3. sustained workloads belong on Fargate
239	```
240	
241	A numbered list restates each hop as its own GT-headed one-hop chain, which reads as several incomplete chains rather than one complete one — the intermediate steps stop being connected to the conclusion they build toward.
242	
243	**Non-conforming — an input carrying unparenthesized prose:**
244	
245	```text
246	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2's threshold
247	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
248	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
249	```
250	
251	`C2's threshold` is not an identifier — it is a possessive prose phrase — so the head does not parse; the third input must be written `C2 (threshold)`.
252	
253	**Conforming — the same head with the upstream chain as an input:**
254	
255	```text
256	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2 (threshold)
257	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
258	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
259	```
260	
261	Exactly one token differs from the block above: a `Cn` identifier with a parenthesized gloss is an admissible head input, on equal footing with a `GT-N` identifier.
262	
263	**Conforming — a chain consuming only upstream conclusions:**
264	
265	```text
266	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold) + C4 (unconditional, zero code change) + C5 (~73% ceiling, no execution-model change)
267	→ C4 and C5 deliver verified savings that do not depend on any property of your workload
268	→ C2's saving depends entirely on a duty-cycle figure nobody has measured
269	```
270	
271	A head may consist entirely of `Cn` inputs with no `GT-N` term. The second hop's `C2's saving` is prose, not a head input — the head-only scope note is what permits it here.
272	
273	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same prose input in a non-final position:**
274	
275	```text
276	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + C2's threshold + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown)
277	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
278	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
279	```
280	
281	This head breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with a well-formed input still to its right the check matches from `GT-12?` onward and never reaches `C2's threshold`. Write `C2 (threshold)` wherever the input sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
282	
283	**Non-conforming — a hop beginning with a GT-N identifier:**
284	
285	```text
286	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
287	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
288	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
289	```
290	
291	The second line reads as the head of a new chain because it begins with a `GT-N` identifier, so this chain ends after its head and what remains is an incomplete chain — the possessive is not the problem, the leading identifier is.
292	
293	**Conforming — the same hop with the identifier moved off the front:**
294	
295	```text
296	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
297	→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates
298	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
299	```
300	
301	Exactly one clause is reordered and the chain is whole again; naming a ground truth inside a hop is fine, leading with its identifier is not.
302	
303	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the GT-led hop in a later position:**
304	
305	```text
306	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
307	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
308	→ the second reading is the binding one
309	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
310	```
311	
312	This hop breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — the check has already satisfied its two-arrow requirement on the hops that precede it, so the leading identifier ends the chain there without changing the verdict. Write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates` wherever the hop sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
313	
314	**Non-conforming — the first hop closing its own sentence:**
315	
316	```text
317	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
318	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape.
319	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
320	```
321	
322	This chain violates none of R1-R9 — every input parses, every hop states one inference, no hop leads with a `GT-N` identifier — and is scored malformed anyway, because the mechanical form check ends the chain the moment the first hop closes its own sentence, before its two-arrow requirement is satisfied, and never reaches the well-formed hop that follows.
323	
324	**Conforming — the same chain with the first hop's terminal period removed:**
325	
326	```text
327	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
328	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
329	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
330	```
331	
332	Exactly one character differs from the block above: the terminal period. Removing it, and nothing else, restores the two-arrow match the check requires.
333	
334	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same period moved to a later hop:**
335	
336	```text
337	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
338	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
339	→ the migration case does not rest on C1 alone
340	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes.
341	```
342	
343	This block breaks the identical rule one hop later and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with two hops already matched before the closing sentence is reached, the check has satisfied its two-arrow requirement and the sentence-closing period on the third hop has no following line left to block. Write the closing hop with no terminal punctuation wherever it sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
344	
345	**One-inference rule.** A hop states exactly ONE inference. If a hop joins two claims with "and", or carries a parenthetical that could stand as its own claim, it is two hops — split it.
346	
347	TELL (not the rule): a hop past ~200 characters is almost always two hops. Measure the hop, then split — do not wrap it, and do not trim words to hit a number.
348	
349	Inline annotations (`*[Assumes: A14 — …]*`) attach to the end of the hop line they qualify and do not start a new hop.
350	
351	### Converting structured-technique outputs into chains
352	
353	Structured-technique outputs (trade-off matrices, second-order effect lists) do not appear in this section as-is — each converts into the chain format above using the rule for its technique below. This subsection is the single source of truth for the conversion; the per-technique Handoff sections point back here rather than restating it, so future structured techniques extend this one place.
354	
355	**Trade-off matrix → one chain.** A trade-off matrix collapses into ONE chain whose intermediate cites the winning weighted total and whose endpoint names a single recommended option:
356	
357	```text
358	GT-refs (criteria's factual basis) → weighted totals (the winning total vs. the runner-up, naming the high-weight criteria that drive it) → recommended option
359	```
360	
361	Example: `GT-2 + GT-5 (criteria facts) → weighted totals: B=82 > A=64, driven by reliability×warranty → recommend B`. The full matrix stays in the technique's own output — this subsection carries only the single collapsed chain, never the matrix re-expressed row-by-row (that would violate the one-chain-per-conclusion rule above). An exact tie between weighted totals still resolves to a single named recommended option; a tie must not produce a multi-option chain endpoint. **Exact-tie tiebreak (deterministic):** on an exact tie, prefer the option with fewer `GT-N?` (unverified) inputs among its winning criteria; if still tied, name both totals in the chain intermediate but select the first-listed option as the chain endpoint, and flag the tie explicitly in the Conclusion section's confidence line.
362	
363	**Second-order effect list → order-marked extension.** A second-order effect list extends the parent chain IN PLACE as additional order-marked steps, each carrying the same evidentiary discipline as the first-order steps that produced the conclusion:
364	
365	```text
366	GT-N → first-order conclusion →[2nd] [2nd-order effect] →[3rd] [3rd-order effect] (contradicts GT-M → back to Phase 2)
367	```
368	
369	Example: `GT-1 → first-order conclusion →[2nd] flag-config surface grows →[3rd] flag debt accumulates (contradicts GT-4 → back to P2)`. The order marks (`[2nd]`, `[3rd]`) make the extension's sequence legible. A contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2 — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2. A pass that surfaces no non-contradicting downstream effect leaves the parent chain unextended — a clean no-op, not an error.
370	
371	### Confidence levels, defined
372	
373	`HIGH`, `MEDIUM` and `LOW` name how much of a chain is **outstanding** — not how strongly the analysis believes its conclusion. Three axes decide the band, each answerable by inspecting what the chain already carries on the page:
374	
375	- **Inputs** — the provenance of every identifier on the head line: an unsuffixed `GT-N` with a named read-at-source location, a `?`-marked ground truth, or a `Cn` carrying its own band.
376	- **Inference** — whether each hop the chain's endpoint depends on follows from the line above it, or needs a premise supplied by an `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation.
377	- **Rivals** — whether a competing conclusion from the same ground truths survives, and what rules it out. Section 5 is where the ruling-out is written down, so a chain answers this axis by pointing at its own Abandoned Reasoning entry as readily as by carrying the rival on its confidence line.
378	
379	**The band is the lowest the three axes license.** A chain is not HIGH because two of them are clean.
380	
381	**HIGH — nothing on this chain is outstanding.** Every identifier on the head line is an unsuffixed `GT-N` whose read-at-source location is named, or a `Cn` itself rated HIGH; every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity cited to an unsuffixed ground truth; and the strongest rival conclusion the analysis considered is named — on this confidence line or in a section 5 entry this chain points to — together with the ground truth or chain that rules it out, that ruling-out input itself unsuffixed. A chain whose endpoint a live alternative still contests is unexamined, not certain: it is MEDIUM at best.
382	
383	An `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation on a hop shorts the Inference axis **unless** the confidence line says what becomes of the endpoint when that assumption fails and the endpoint still stands — *"A2 is that the CDN'd assets are versioned; if they were not, the CDN result would be weaker evidence still, so the conclusion is unaffected"*. An annotation on a hop that only qualifies a second-order extension, and not the endpoint, is outside this axis and the chain says which case it is. Stating the sensitivity is the work; an unexamined assumption is not the same thing as one whose falsity has been priced.
384	
385	The Rivals axis is answered when a section 5 entry names a competing conclusion to this chain's endpoint and the chain or ground truth that ruled it out, or when the endpoint is itself a ruling-out — a chain establishing that some option does not work has already done the rival's work and does not need a rival of its own. It is short when a competing conclusion has been raised anywhere in the analysis and nothing settles it, and when the analysis reaches a positive recommendation with no section 5 content bearing on it at all.
386	
387	**MEDIUM — exactly one axis is short, and the shortfall is named and bounded.** One of: an identifier on the head line is `?`-marked or is a `Cn` rated MEDIUM; or at most one hop the endpoint depends on rests on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise whose failure the chain has not priced; or a rival to the endpoint is live and nothing in the analysis settles it. The confidence line names which axis is short, names the specific input, hop or rival, and states what would close it — the verification that would remove an input as a cause of the downgrade, the evidence that would establish an assumed premise, or the observation that would settle between this conclusion and its rival. A MEDIUM chain is one whose weakness a reader can point at.
388	
389	**LOW — the shortfall is unbounded, or more than one axis is short.** Two or more axes short at once; or an input is `?` with no verification path available; or a hop's missing premise cannot be stated as an assumption at all, so the analysis cannot say what would make the step valid; or a rival survives that no available observation would settle. A LOW chain is reportable, and a conclusion resting on it alone is not actionable.
390	
391	**Calibration rule.** Each rating is the highest its inputs, hops and rivals license, **and no higher**. Rating above what the axes license over-claims. Rating below it is a defect of the same kind: a chain meeting HIGH on all three axes and written MEDIUM misreports the analysis's own strength, and a document whose every chain carries the same defensive band tells a reader nothing about which parts to trust. Criterion 5 scores calibration, not altitude — an analysis whose every band is the one its axes license is Rigorous whether its conclusion is HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW.
392	
393	**The caps are consequences, not extra rules.** The unverified-input rule (D-07) below and the ceiling at the lowest-rated chain a head cites are what the Inputs axis says, restated for the two cases that occur most often; they are the fast check, and these definitions are what they check for. A cap never licenses a band on its own — it bounds from above, and the band is still the lowest any of the three axes licenses.
394	
395	**Confidence pre-check (Inputs axis).** Directly above every `**Confidence:**` line — each §4 chain's and the §6 Conclusion's — write one `**Pre-check:**` line, with nothing between it and the `**Confidence:**` line it checks:
396	
397	```text
398	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-3?, C2 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: GT-3? · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
399	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-3? is unverified; …
400	```
401	
402	Four fields, separated by ` · `: `head` lists every identifier on the chain's head line (the part before the first `→`), in order, comma-separated, a `?` suffix kept (`GT-3?`), each `Cn` followed by its own stated band in parentheses (`C2 (MEDIUM)`) — for the §6 roll-up, `head` is every chain the Conclusion rests on, each with its band, plus any `GT-N?` the Conclusion rests on directly. `?-marked` lists the `?`-suffixed identifiers from `head`, comma-separated, or the token `none`. `lowest cited` is the lowest band among the `Cn` in `head`, or `none` when `head` cites no chain. `Inputs ceiling` is the Inputs axis's bound: `LOW` if `lowest cited` is LOW; otherwise `MEDIUM` if `?-marked` is not `none` or `lowest cited` is MEDIUM; otherwise `HIGH`.
403	
404	This is the Inputs axis of "Confidence levels, defined" made procedural — Inference and Rivals are not scored on this line, and can only lower the band further. The ceiling bounds from above, as the caps-are-consequences paragraph above states; the `**Confidence:**` label may equal it or sit below it, and never above it — a below-ceiling label is explained by the Confidence line itself, not by the pre-check. In §6, the pre-check line is itself a Conclusion-section claim under the Claim inventory rule below, and it is cited by the chains its own `head` names.
405	
406	### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]
407	
408	GT-N ([brief fact label, source]) + GT-M ([brief fact label, source])
409	→ [intermediate claim — a new inference statable from combining GT-N and GT-M but from neither alone]
410	→ [conclusion — the claim this chain establishes]
411	
412	**Pre-check:** head [every head identifier; each Cn with its band, e.g. C2 (MEDIUM)] · ?-marked: [the GT-N? identifiers, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest Cn band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
413	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
414	[If MEDIUM or LOW: name each GT-N? input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; name each Cn on this chain's head rated below HIGH, which need not be re-explained here; and give each downgrade cause belonging to this chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists (the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause).]
415	
416	**Unverified input rule (D-07):** A chain that includes any `GT-N?` input must end with a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line. The line must name the unverified input and state the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. A HIGH confidence claim cannot rest on an unverified ground truth. A chain is also rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites — the stated confidence label of each `Cn` on its head line, the part before the first `→`. This is a ceiling: it bounds the rating from above and is never a reason to rate a chain HIGH, and a cited chain rated MEDIUM under a validation-rubric EXCEPT clause still caps every chain that cites it. Every MEDIUM or LOW confidence line explains only its own chain's rating, so its validity never depends on how far away a cap originates. The line names each `GT-N?` input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. It names each `Cn` on the chain's head rated below HIGH and need not re-explain that `Cn`, whose own confidence line carries the explanation, so no line has to trace a cited chain's lineage. 306	source citations, and a provenance label, with unverified and delegate-reported entries marked

309	**Provenance check (apply before banding).** A citation being present is not verification. For
310	each unsuffixed ground truth, ask whether the analysis read the asserted figure in the cited
311	source — `read-at-source` — or merely received it from a sub-agent, search result, or summary
312	without opening the citation (`reported-by-delegate`, which requires the `?`). Score against

316	  the identifiers referenced in the Derivation Chains section; every verified GT has a source

325	  by that record naming which source and why unreachable.

346	  delegate-reported) is used without the `?` suffix **and it feeds only MEDIUM or LOW

379	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).
380	Both sections are in scope for this criterion. Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration, or hop validity and arithmetic — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.

384	- **Rigorous** — every conclusion stated anywhere in the document (in section 4 or section 6)
385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning

594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.

596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
597	
598	A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
599	
600	---
601	
602	## Usage Note
603	
604	Score every criterion. Produce one verdict block per criterion, using the prescribed format
605	from the Verdict Block Format section above. The analysis must clear the gate (no criterion
606	at Absent) and the hand-wavy cap (at most one criterion at Hand-wavy) before conclusions are
607	presented. If either condition is not met, revise the relevant sections and re-score — bounded
608	to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under "How to
609	Apply This Gate" at the top of this document. If a criterion still fails after that single
610	pass, present it as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of re-scoring
611	again. This closing note restates that bound; it does not create a second, looser one.

3	# Trade-Off Analysis
4	
5	> Structures a choice between two or more genuinely viable options by weighting
6	> criteria before scoring — preventing the reverse-engineering of weights to
7	> justify a decision already made intuitively.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to reach for this
12	
13	Use this tool when two or more options are viable (none obviously dominant), the
14	choice spans multiple criteria that pull in different directions, and an
15	intuitive pick would be hard to justify to others.
16	
17	Do not use it when one option dominates on every relevant criterion — that is a
18	direct decision, not a trade-off.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## Procedure
23	
24	1. **Name the options — including the status quo.** List each option being
25	   compared, and **always include doing nothing** as one of them, named as what
26	   it concretely is ("keep the current 70/30 split", "stay on REST/JSON"). A
27	   comparison whose option set is all-change silently assumes change is
28	   warranted and reports that assumption back as a finding. If the status quo is
29	   genuinely unavailable — a contract expires, the hardware is failing — say so
30	   in one line and list it as ruled out; do not omit it silently. **Include a
31	   composite too:** when the named options can be split or combined — part of
32	   one and part of another, or one now and another later — list at least one
33	   such composite as its own option. A comparison limited to the options as the
34	   question named them cannot find that a mix of them is best. If the options
35	   genuinely cannot combine, say why in one line and list the composite as ruled
36	   out; do not omit it silently.
37	
38	2. **State the must-haves and apply them as knock-outs.** Before any scoring,
39	   name the conditions an option must satisfy to be viable at all. An option
40	   that fails a must-have is **eliminated, not scored low** — report it under
41	   `## Options` as knocked out, with the must-have it failed. Scoring a
42	   non-viable option lets a high weighted total out-vote a hard constraint,
43	   which is how an option that cannot actually be chosen wins a trade-off.
44	   If nothing is a must-have, write "no must-haves" rather than skipping the
45	   step — the two are different claims.
46	
47	3. **List criteria.** Identify 5–8 criteria that matter to this decision. Lock
48	   this list — add no new criteria after this step. If a criterion matters, it
49	   must appear now.
50	
51	4. **Assign weights. Lock them now.** Give each criterion a relative weight
52	   (1–5) before scoring any option. If you cannot assign weights without first
53	   seeing how options score, stop — locking weights before scoring is the core
54	   discipline that prevents reverse-engineering them to favor an intuitive pick.
55	
56	5. **Anchor the scale, then score.** Before scoring, state for each criterion
57	   what a **1** and a **5** concretely mean — the anchors. "Cost: 1 = over
58	   $20k, 5 = under $2k" is an anchor; "Cost: 1 = bad, 5 = good" is not. Then
59	   score each option on each criterion independently (1–5) against those
60	   anchors. Phrase every criterion so higher is always better (e.g.,
61	   "Reliability" not "Reliability risk") — a mixed scale silently inverts the
62	   result. Without anchors a score means only "how I felt about this option",
63	   and the arithmetic that follows inherits that and dresses it as a number.
64	
65	6. **Cite the ground truth each score rests on.** Every score names the
66	   `GT-ID`s that justify it. A score resting on a `GT-N?` input carries that
67	   `?` forward: per D-07, the chain this trade-off collapses into is capped at
68	   **MEDIUM** and its confidence line names the unverified input and the
69	   verification that would remove it. A score with no ground truth behind it is
70	   a preference — mark it as one rather than citing nothing.
71	
72	7. **Compute:** multiply weight × score per criterion; sum per option.
73	
74	8. **Read the result.** The highest weighted total among the surviving options
75	   is the recommendation. If it surprises you, only re-examine a weight when you
76	   can state why it was wrong *before* seeing the result — adjusting weights
77	   afterward is the failure mode this procedure prevents.
78	
79	**Flip test — run it every time, not only on a near-tie.** Report the
80	**smallest weight change that changes the winner**: name the criterion, the
81	weight it would have to move to, and how far that is from the weight you
82	locked. Then ask whether that weight is genuinely wrong. A winner that survives
83	only a ±1 move on one criterion is a near-tie whatever the totals look like,
84	and a winner that survives every single-criterion move is a robust result —
85	both are findings, and neither is visible from the totals alone. Report the
86	flip distance under `## Recommendation`. Do not refine scores to break a
87	near-tie; refining manufactures false precision. If no single-criterion change
88	flips the result, say that explicitly — "no single weight change flips this"
89	is the strongest result this procedure can return, and it is worth stating.
90	
91	---
92	
93	## Example
94	
95	**Decision:** Laptop for a parent who browses, video-calls, and writes
96	documents.
97	
98	**Ground truths this rests on:**
99	
100	- **GT-1** — the current machine drops video calls roughly weekly (observed over
101	  two months).
102	- **GT-2** — refurbished units from this vendor carry a 90-day warranty; new
103	  units carry 12 months (vendor's published terms, read at source).
104	- **GT-3?** — refurbished failure rates are "around twice" new in the first
105	  year. *Unverified — recalled from a review article, source not located.*
106	
107	**Step 1 — options named, status quo included:**
108	
109	- **A** — refurbished mid-range
110	- **B** — new entry-level
111	- **C** — keep the current laptop (status quo)
112	
113	**Step 2 — must-haves applied as knock-outs:**
114	
115	| Must-have | A | B | C |
116	|---|---|---|---|
117	| Holds a video call without dropping | ✓ | ✓ | **✗ (GT-1)** |
118	
119	**C is knocked out, not scored.** Had it been scored instead, its perfect cost
120	score (5 × 3 = 15, nothing to spend) would have carried it close to A on a
121	total — while still failing the one thing the machine is being replaced *for*.
122	This is the failure mode step 2 exists to prevent.
123	
124	**Steps 3-4 — criteria and weights locked before any scoring:**
125	
126	| Criterion                       | Weight | 1 means…                    | 5 means…                     |
127	|----------------------------------|--------|-----------------------------|------------------------------|
128	| Performance                      | 4      | stutters on a video call    | headroom for years           |
129	| Reliability                      | 5      | failure expected in year 1  | failure unlikely in 5 years  |
130	| Cost                             | 3      | over $900                   | under $300                   |
131	| Warranty / support               | 4      | none                        | 12 months or more            |
132	| Portability                      | 2      | desk-bound                  | carried daily without thought|
133	| Ease of setup (non-technical)    | 3      | needs a technical helper    | works out of the box         |
134	
135	**Step 5-7 — scored against those anchors, with the ground truth behind each:**
136	
137	| Option     | Performance (×4) | Reliability (×5) | Cost (×3)  | Warranty (×4) | Portability (×2) | Ease of setup (×3) | Total  |
138	|------------|------------------|------------------|------------|---------------|------------------|--------------------|--------|
139	| A (refurb) | 4 × 4 = 16       | 2 × 5 = 10       | 5 × 3 = 15 | 2 × 4 = 8     | 3 × 2 = 6        | 3 × 3 = 9          | **64** |
140	| B (new)    | 2 × 4 = 8        | 5 × 5 = 25       | 3 × 3 = 9  | 5 × 4 = 20    | 4 × 2 = 8        | 4 × 3 = 12         | **82** |
141	
142	Reliability scores rest on **GT-3?**; warranty scores on **GT-2**.
143	
144	**Step 8 — result:** B scores 82 vs. A's 64, a gap of 18, driven by reliability
145	and warranty.
146	
147	**Flip test:** no single weight change within the 1–5 scale flips this result.
148	The closest is Reliability 5 → 1, which closes the gap from 18 to 6 — and that
149	move means asserting reliability barely matters for a machine bought *because*
150	the current one fails. Every other single-criterion move leaves a wider gap
151	(Warranty 4 → 1 leaves 9; Cost 3 → 5 leaves 14). The recommendation is robust
152	in the sense this test can establish.
153	
154	**Confidence:** MEDIUM, not HIGH. Reliability carries the heaviest weight (5)
155	and its scores rest on **GT-3?**, which is unverified — so per D-07 the chain
156	this collapses into is capped at MEDIUM. Locating a failure-rate figure in the
157	vendor's own return data, or a cited reliability study, would remove that cause.
158	Note what the flip test does *not* do here: it varies weights, not scores, so a
159	robust flip result does not repair an unverified input.
160	
161	---
162	
163	## Failure modes
164	
165	- **Weights set after scoring.** If you scored options before assigning
166	  weights, the weights will unconsciously reflect the scores — discard and
167	  restart from step 4.
168	
169	- **Too many criteria.** More than 8 criteria dilute the signal toward noise —
170	  prune to those that genuinely differentiate the options.
171	
172	- **Criteria added mid-analysis.** Adding a criterion after seeing partial
173	  scores is almost always rationalizing — lock the list at step 3 and restart.
174	
175	- **Treating a near-tie as a precision problem.** Refining scores to break a
176	  near-tie manufactures false precision; run the flip test instead.
177	
178	- **Criteria that are not independent.** Two criteria measuring the same factor
179	  (e.g., "cost" and "budget impact") double-count it — merge or drop one.
180	
181	- **The status quo left off the option list.** An all-change option set assumes
182	  change is warranted and then reports that assumption as a finding. Doing
183	  nothing is an option until a stated must-have rules it out (step 1).
184	
185	- **A must-have scored instead of applied.** Scoring a non-viable option lets a
186	  high weighted total out-vote a hard constraint, so an option that cannot
187	  actually be chosen can win. Knock it out at step 2 and say which must-have it
188	  failed.
189	
190	- **Unanchored scores.** Without stated 1-and-5 anchors a score records how the
191	  option felt, and the arithmetic launders that into a number. Anchors are what
192	  make two options comparable — and the same analysis reproducible.
193	
194	- **The flip test skipped because the totals look decisive.** A wide gap can
195	  still rest on one weight. Run the test every time; "no single weight change
196	  flips this" is a real and reportable result, not a null one.
197	
198	- **A robust flip result read as confidence in the inputs.** The flip test
199	  varies *weights*, not scores. It says nothing about whether a `GT-N?` behind a
200	  score is true, and never lifts D-07's cap.
201	
202	---
203	
204	## Output contract
205	
206	The focused trade-off output MUST include these four level-2 section headers, verbatim,
207	as real `##` headings in the response. Strict on the header strings; soft on content.
208	This structure enables reliable downstream detection.
209	
210	Required headers:
211	
212	- `## Options`
213	- `## Criteria & Weights`
214	- `## Scoring`
215	- `## Recommendation`
216	
217	---
218	
219	## Handoff
220	
221	The output is the recommended option with its weighted justification and the
222	reasoning behind the weights. Return to Phase 4 (Reason Upward) and convert it
223	into the Derivation Chain using the trade-off collapse form defined in
224	output-template.md §4 ("Converting structured-technique outputs into chains") —
225	citing the weighted scores as the step between ground truths and conclusion.

3	# Pre-Mortem
4	
5	> A prospective-hindsight failure analysis tool. Reach for this when a proposed
6	> plan needs stress-testing before commitment — the goal is to surface probable
7	> failure causes before they materialise.
8	
9	---
10	
11	## When to reach for this
12	
13	Use a pre-mortem once a plan has enough specificity to reason about particular
14	failure modes, but before it is finalised and carries organizational momentum.
15	Not the right tool for evaluating options (use trade-off analysis) or for tracing
16	something that already went wrong (use 5-Whys).
17	
18	**Decision rule — pre-mortem vs. inversion:** pre-mortem stress-tests a **plan**;
19	[inversion](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/inversion.md) stress-tests a **claim**. If a concrete plan with actions and a
20	timeline exists, pre-mortem is the right tool — it reasons about implementation failure
21	modes that claim-level inversion cannot see. With only a stated belief, conclusion, or
22	design principle in hand, inversion fits better. This is the same boundary
23	`inversion.md` states from its own side, and it is the one that matters most here:
24	Phase 5 selects between these two directly, so a reader arriving from that
25	prescription needs to know why they were sent here rather than there.
26	
27	---
28	
29	## Framing
30	
31	Before any other step, adopt this premise explicitly:
32	
33	> It is approximately six months from now. This plan has failed — not merely
34	> underperformed, but failed badly. That outcome is a fact.
35	> Working backward: what caused it?
36	
37	This past-tense framing is not rhetorical. It bypasses the optimism bias that
38	makes forward-looking risk lists generic. Do not skip it or soften it to
39	"might fail" — the grammatical shift from possibility to accomplished fact is
40	the mechanism.
41	
42	---
43	
44	## Procedure
45	
46	1. **Restate the premise.** Before writing anything, say or write: "The plan has
47	   already failed. What caused it?" This re-anchors the prospective-hindsight
48	   frame before analysis begins.
49	
50	2. **Write independently.** List every cause of the failure without filtering —
51	   write the full list before reviewing it. Do not discard causes that seem
52	   unlikely; the list is raw material, not a verdict. Generate from at least
53	   three named viewpoints — for example the implementer, the person who has to
54	   live with the result, whoever pays for it, and a competitor who benefits
55	   from the failure. One generator asked once returns one perspective's
56	   failures, and the causes it misses are systematically the ones outside the
57	   frame it was asked in.
58	
59	3. **Interrogate the list adversarially.** Re-read each item and ask which ones
60	   contradict the plan's own stated premise, or the recommendation the analysis
61	   is about to make. A cause that would embarrass the conclusion is higher
62	   signal than one that merely adds risk to it. In a facilitated session these
63	   are the items a junior participant suppresses; written by a single analyst
64	   they are the items that get hedged into vagueness rather than dropped, so
65	   look for the softened ones, not the missing ones.
66	
67	4. **Identify recurring patterns.** Look for failure causes that cluster — the
68	   same root (over-optimistic timeline, single point of dependency, assumption
69	   never validated). A cluster is a structural weakness in the plan, not an
70	   isolated risk.
71	
72	5. **Triage each cluster on two axes: plausibility and recoverability.** Not by
73	   a probability figure invented for the purpose — say which of these it is:
74	
75	   - **Fatal** — if it happens, the plan does not recover. These get a plan
76	     change, not a mitigation, however unlikely they seem.
77	   - **Costly but survivable** — the plan continues at a stated price. These get
78	     a mitigation and an owner.
79	   - **Tolerable** — record and move on.
80	
81	   Sort by recoverability *before* plausibility. A fatal-but-unlikely cause
82	   outranks a likely-but-tolerable one, and ranking by likelihood alone inverts
83	   exactly that comparison — which is the failure a pre-mortem exists to catch.
84	
85	6. **Give every fatal and costly cluster a tripwire.** A tripwire is the
86	   **observation that would tell you this failure is now underway**, named in
87	   advance: a threshold, a date, a signal, a metric crossing a line. "Watch
88	   integration risk" is not a tripwire; "the staging sync job fails twice in one
89	   week" is, and "we have not got a test environment by 14 March" is.
90	
91	   State who would see it and when they would look. A failure mode nobody is
92	   positioned to notice has no tripwire, and saying so plainly is more useful
93	   than writing one that will never fire. The pre-mortem's value is spent at the
94	   moment the list is written unless something converts a predicted failure into
95	   a detected one — that is what the tripwire is.
96	
97	7. **Act on findings.** Modify the plan to address the structural weaknesses, or
98	   explicitly accept the risk with a named mitigation. A pre-mortem with no
99	   downstream plan change was box-ticking.
100	
101	**Exit criterion:** The failure has been stated as having already happened, causes
102	are written from that stance, causes are clustered into structural weaknesses,
103	every cluster carries a triage verdict of fatal / costly but survivable /
104	tolerable, every fatal and costly cluster carries a tripwire with an owner or an
105	explicit statement that no observable one exists, and every cluster has either a
106	named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk with a named mitigation. A
107	pre-mortem that ends without one of those two outcomes per cluster is
108	box-ticking, not a finding.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## Output contract
113	
114	The exit criterion above names four things the pre-mortem must produce. This is
115	what they look like on the page, in this order:
116	
117	**Premise** — one line, past tense, stating the failure as accomplished fact.
118	Not "the plan might fail"; the grammatical shift is the mechanism, and a premise
119	written in the conditional has already lost it.
120	
121	**Causes** — the unfiltered list, one per line, written before any grouping
122	appears. The viewpoints from step 2 are visible in it: if every cause is a
123	technical one, step 2 was run once rather than three times. Writing the clusters
124	first and back-filling causes into them inverts the procedure and produces the
125	generic risk list the whole framing exists to avoid.
126	
127	**Clusters** — the structural weaknesses the causes fall into, each named, and
128	each naming the causes it absorbs. A cluster is a claim that several causes share
129	one root; a heading with one cause under it is a cause, not a cluster. When the
130	pre-mortem runs inside a first-principles analysis, each cluster also cites the
131	chain ids (`Cn`) or ground-truth ids (`GT-N`) it bears on, so the finding lands
132	somewhere a reader can check it against.
133	
134	**Disposition** — per cluster, one of exactly two things: a named plan change, or
135	an explicitly accepted risk with a named mitigation. "Worth watching", "we should
136	keep this in mind" and "a risk we accept" with nothing named after it are none of
137	the above. A cluster whose disposition is an accepted risk still names what makes
138	the risk survivable; that is what distinguishes accepting a risk from noticing one.
139	
140	A pre-mortem missing any of the four has not run. A pre-mortem whose causes list
141	is shorter than its cluster list ran backwards.
142	
143	---
144	
145	## Example
146	
147	**Plan:** Host a dinner party for twelve people in two weeks, cooking a full
148	three-course meal from scratch for the first time at this scale.
149	
150	**Framing applied:** It is two weeks from now. The dinner party has failed badly.
151	What caused it?
152	
153	**Backward-derived failure causes:**
154	- Underestimated preparation time; last two courses were served an hour late
155	- A key ingredient unavailable the day before; no substitution plan
156	- One course required equipment not owned and not sourced in advance
157	- Two guests had dietary restrictions not asked about until the day of
158	- Energy depleted by the time guests arrived; host unable to enjoy the evening
159	
160	**Pattern identified:** Every cause traces back to a single structural weakness —
161	no dry run at smaller scale and no contingency check before commitment. The plan
162	assumed novelty would resolve itself on the day.
163	
164	---
165	
166	## Failure modes
167	
168	**Forward-looking framing.** "What could go wrong?" produces a generic risk list.
169	If causes feel speculative and mild, the past-tense premise was not adopted.
170	
171	**Running it too early.** A pre-mortem on a plan with insufficient specificity
172	yields generic concerns. The plan must have enough detail to reason about
173	particular failure modes — vague plans produce vague analyses.
174	
175	**Anchoring (in group settings).** When facilitated, the most senior voice in the
176	room shapes the list. Run independent writing before any sharing — each
177	participant writes silently before the group compares lists.
178	
179	**First-speaker anchoring.** The first cause named draws subsequent thinking
180	toward it. Write exhaustively before ranking or grouping.
181	
182	**No follow-through.** A pre-mortem with no downstream plan change was
183	box-ticking. Findings must modify the plan or be explicitly accepted with
184	named mitigations.
185	
186	---
187	
188	## Handoff
189	
190	The probable failure causes identified here feed Phase 5 (Validate). Add the
191	highest-signal structural weaknesses to the adversarial validation pass — each
192	one is a weak-link candidate for the signed-off analysis to address or explicitly
193	accept.
